title: Graphs of Power and Exponential Functions
seo_title: Sec 3 Power and exponential graphs Worksheets: Free Secondary 3 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: graphs of power functions y = axⁿ, where n = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, and simple sums of not more than three of these; graphs of exponential functions y = kaˣ, where a is a positive integer, a > 1; estimation of the gradient of a curve by drawing a tangent
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 maths worksheets on graphs of power functions y = axⁿ, reciprocal graphs, exponential graphs y = kaˣ, tables of values and the gradient of a curve using a tangent. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Know the shapes: x², x³, 1/x, 1/x² and kaˣ each have their own graph.
key_sub: The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of its tangent: rise ÷ run.
body_html:
How it works

  • y = ax²: a parabola. y = ax³: an S-shaped cubic through the origin.
  • y = a/x: two curves in opposite quadrants. y = a/x²: two curves on the same side of the x-axis. Neither touches the axes.
  • y = kaˣ (a > 1): always above the x-axis, cuts the y-axis at (0, k), and grows faster and faster.
  • The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent there: rise ÷ run using two points on the tangent.
Example

Find y when x = −2 for y = x² + 4/x.

(−2)² = 4

4 ÷ (−2) = −2

4 + (−2)

Answer: 2

Example

For y = 3 × 2ˣ, find y when x = 3.

2³ = 8

3 × 8

Answer: 24

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up y = 1/x (opposite quadrants) and y = 1/x² (both above the x-axis).
  • Working out 2ˣ as 2 × x. 2³ = 8, not 6.
  • Squaring a negative number wrongly: (−3)² = 9, but (−3)³ = −27.
  • Using run ÷ rise for the gradient, or reading the gradient off the curve instead of the tangent.

faq.q: What do power graphs look like?
faq.a: y = x² is a ∪-shaped parabola, y = x³ is an S-shaped curve, y = 1/x has two branches in opposite quadrants, and y = 1/x² has two branches above the x-axis.

faq.q: What does an exponential graph look like?
faq.a: y = kaˣ with a > 1 stays above the x-axis, passes through (0, k) and rises more and more steeply as x increases.

faq.q: How do you estimate the gradient of a curve?
faq.a: Draw the tangent touching the curve at the point, choose two points on the tangent far apart, and divide the change in y by the change in x.

faq.q: Why does y = 1/x never touch the axes?
faq.a: x cannot be 0, because you cannot divide by 0, and 1/x is never 0, so the curve gets closer to the axes without touching them.
